text: Someone assumes Claw judges. Is this a problem by feel? It doesn't decide, it checks. A written skill spells out exactly what counts as a problem. Liam walks you through it. A skill is a folder Claude reads before it acts. This one is called, "Is this a problem?" It's skill. MD holds the whole instruction set in plain language. No hidden logic. Nothing left to guess. Claude reads the file, then follows it. The file is the program. Inside a step section lays out the pipeline. Read the situation. Check it against a list of defined conditions. Then answer. Watch that middle step, the checklist. It isn't Claude weighing the

Situation on its own. It's Claude matching it against conditions someone already wrote down. Back to that checklist. Feed it a situation the list anticipated and it answers the same way every time. Reliable on repeat. But feed it something the list never named and it has nothing to fall back on. Not wrong exactly, just outside what the spec covers. That's the trade a written checklist makes. Consistency where it applies. silence everywhere else. Is this a problem from Claude? Means, is this a problem according to the checklist it was given? Same input, same output every run. And only for what that checklist thought to name. Your turn.

Here's the prompt. Read it with me. Pick one decision you currently make by gut feel. Is this urgent? Is this worth escalating? Is this a problem? Ask Claw to help you write out the actual criteria you're using as a short checklist. Then run your next three real cases through it and flag anything that doesn't fit. Lay them in for bear. Claude, is this a problem? Liam in for bear.
